name: Intro to Boxing — Session 1
intent: First exposure: establish a base, a guard, and one punch. No contact beyond a held mitt.
coach_notes: Deliberately short on content. First sessions fail from volume, not from too little material.

name: Beginner Footwork
intent: Build step-drag and lateral movement before any punch is attached to them.

name: Beginner Straight Punches
intent: Jab and cross from a stable base, with the weight transfer taught before the rear hand.

name: Intermediate Movement and Angles
intent: Pivot and angle-cutting against a moving reference.

name: Intermediate Combinations — Random Practice
intent: Combination work with sequences called at random rather than blocked, following the contextual-interference retention evidence.
coach_notes: Random calling is deliberate. Blocked practice looks better in the session and retains worse — though note the contextual-interference evidence is contested in applied settings.

name: Defensive Foundations
intent: Catch, parry, slip and roll at controlled speed, each linked back to guard.

name: Conditioned Sparring Session
intent: Single-task conditioned sparring with defined roles. Requires coach authorization and confirmed eligibility.
coach_notes: No sparring volume is prescribed. The coach sets rounds and intensity in person, against this athlete on this day, with medical and eligibility status confirmed by qualified humans.

name: Adaptive Session — Seated Base
intent: Technical boxing from a seated or supported base, with range set to the athlete.
coach_notes: Not a reduced version of a standing session. Base is defined with the athlete; the technical target is the same.

name: Non-Contact Fitness Boxing
intent: Boxing-style conditioning for participants not pursuing contact. A complete lane, not a preparatory stage.

name: Strength and Power Support
intent: Off-floor strength supporting boxing demands, balancing the pushing volume boxing accumulates.
coach_notes: Horizontal pull is included specifically to offset punching and pressing volume.

name: Advanced Tactical Problem Solving
intent: Imposed tactical problems with the athlete identifying and addressing them.

name: Youth Session — Movement and Play
intent: Youth-appropriate session prioritising movement variety and engagement over technical volume.
coach_notes: Content is deliberately light. Youth retention is an engagement problem before it is a technical one.

WHAT THIS SESSION IS","lines":["This is an active recovery workout for a boxer who trained hard the day before, especially after a session like a weighted bag routine, speed-endurance session, shoulder-fatigue session, hard mitts, sparring, or any workout that stressed the upper body, nervous system, and technical sharpness.","This is not a conditioning workout.","This is not a toughness workout.","This is not a “sweat as much as possible” workout.","This is not a replacement for hard training.","This is a session designed to help the athlete recover better while still moving, so that the next real training day can be higher quality.","A lot of fighters make the mistake of thinking recovery means either:","doing absolutely nothing, or","doing another hard workout and calling it “light”","Both mistakes can slow progress.","A proper active recovery day sits in the middle. It gives the body enough movement to:","improve circulation","reduce stiffness","restore joint motion","reinforce clean technique","calm the nervous system","help the athlete feel more athletic again","The result should be that the boxer finishes the session feeling:","looser","sharper","less tense","more coordinated","more ready for the next hard day","If the athlete finishes this workout exhausted, burned out, or mentally drained, then it was not active recovery anymore."]},{"heading":"2. THE TRUE PURPOSE OF ACTIVE RECOVERY","lines":["To understand the workout, it helps to understand the purpose in plain language.","After a hard boxing session, the body is not only tired in one way. Fatigue comes from several places at once.","After yesterday’s weighted bag work, the athlete is likely dealing with:","A. Local muscular fatigue","The shoulders, upper arms, upper back, trunk, and stabilizers worked repeatedly. Even though the punches were light and fast, the repetition volume can create:","shoulder burn","arm heaviness","stiffness","reduced snap in the punches","local fatigue in supporting muscles","B. Nervous system fatigue","Fast punching is not only muscular. It depends heavily on the nervous system. Speed training requires the body to:","fire muscles quickly","coordinate timing","maintain rhythm","stabilize posture","repeat precise actions under fatigue","Even if the workout was not “heavy,” it may still have been neurologically demanding. That is why a boxer can feel “off,” “slow,” “flat,” or “wired but tired” the next day.","C. Joint and connective tissue irritation","Repetitive punching can leave the shoulders, elbows, wrists, scapulae, and thoracic area feeling tight or slightly irritated, especially if technique drifted late in the workout.","D. Technical disruption from fatigue","Once fatigue sets in, technique often changes:","hands return slower","shoulders tense up","hooks get wider","uppercuts start scooping","stance becomes less balanced","breathing becomes more shallow","movement loses fluidity","Active recovery helps clean this up."]},{"heading":"3. WHAT ACTIVE RECOVERY IS SUPPOSED TO DO","lines":["A good active recovery session has several jobs.","Job 1: Increase blood flow without adding new fatigue","Gentle movement helps circulate blood through muscles that are stiff, sore, or fatigued. Better circulation supports the recovery process by helping the body transport oxygen and nutrients while also supporting the clearing of metabolic byproducts.","This does not mean “flush lactic acid” in the oversimplified way people sometimes say it, because lactate itself clears relatively quickly after training. The deeper point is that low-intensity movement supports the overall recovery environment by improving circulation, tissue temperature, and movement quality.","Job 2: Restore range of motion and movement quality","Hard boxing sessions often leave the athlete feeling mechanically “stuck.” The shoulders may feel elevated, the chest tight, the upper back locked, and the hips less free. A recovery session helps reopen clean movement.","Job 3: Downshift the nervous system","Hard training often leaves the athlete in a more “amped” sympathetic state:","higher tension","shallow breathing","reduced relaxation","poor rhythm","feeling wired or agitated","An active recovery session uses low-intensity movement and slower breathing to help the body shift toward a calmer recovery state.","Job 4: Rehearse clean technique under zero pressure","This is important in boxing. On a hard day, technique is tested. On a recovery day, technique is restored. The athlete can rehearse:","guard position","balance","rhythm","breathing","relaxed punching","defensive mechanics","foot placement","without the stress of impact or fatigue buildup.","Job 5: Teach body awareness","Recovery work teaches the athlete to notice:","where tension lives","what fatigue feels like","when movement becomes forced","how breathing affects rhythm","how posture affects punching mechanics","That skill matters because smarter fighters recover better, and fighters who recover better usually train better."]},{"heading":"4. THE SCIENCE OF WHY THIS WORKS","lines":["Here is the science in practical language.","A. Low-intensity movement supports recovery better than total stiffness","After hard training, complete inactivity can sometimes leave a boxer feeling more stiff and sluggish, especially in the shoulders, thoracic spine, hips, and calves. Gentle movement helps maintain circulation and tissue mobility without creating new stress.","B. Recovery depends on total stress load","The body does not only care whether today’s session is “hard” or “easy.” It responds to the total load placed on muscles, joints, and the nervous system over time. If yesterday stressed speed and shoulder endurance, today should reduce overall stress, not sneak in extra work.","C. Technique is easier to restore at low intensity","Motor patterns improve when the athlete can practice cleanly. If an athlete is moving too fast, too hard, or too tired, the nervous system may rehearse bad habits. A recovery session gives the athlete a chance to groove efficient movement.","D. Breathing influences recovery state","Longer exhales and relaxed nasal breathing can help reduce excessive arousal and tension. This matters because many boxers stay in a subtle fight mode after hard training. Breathing drills at the end of a session help signal safety and recovery.","E. Gentle shoulder and scapular work helps punching athletes","Punching athletes often accumulate tension in:","front delts","pecs","upper traps","neck","biceps tendon region","while underusing certain stabilizers in the upper back and scapular control system. Recovery drills that restore scapular movement and posture can help shoulder health and improve the feel of the next punching session.","F. Active recovery protects tomorrow’s performance","The real value of this session is not only how it feels today. The real value is that it helps preserve the quality of the next important day. Good recovery protects:","speed","timing","mechanics","confidence","consistency"]},{"heading":"5. THE NUMBER ONE RULE OF ACTIVE RECOVERY","lines":["The athlete must finish feeling better than they started.","That is the standard.","Not:","“I was drenched in sweat”","“My arms were on fire”","“I pushed through”","“I made it hard anyway”","Instead:","shoulders feel looser","stance feels easier","breathing feels calmer","movement feels smoother","mind feels clearer","If the athlete feels worse at the end, the session was too hard, too long, too tense, or too poorly controlled."]},{"heading":"6. INTENSITY RULES FOR THIS SESSION","lines":["These rules should guide the whole workout.","Effort level","Keep the session around 3 to 5 out of 10 effort.","That means:","you are definitely moving","you are engaged","you are not straining","you could comfortably speak in short sentences","breathing stays under control","nothing feels forced","Speed","Movements can be crisp, but they should not be explosive in a way that creates strain.","Tension","The body should stay loose.","A boxer on active recovery day should not feel like they are trying to dominate the workout. They should feel like they are restoring themselves.","Fatigue","You may feel mildly warm and more alive as the session goes on.","You should not feel progressively depleted."]},{"heading":"7. FULL WORKOUT OVERVIEW","lines":["Total time","About 30 to 45 minutes","Main sections","Warm-up and joint preparation","Light stance and rhythm work","Technical shadowboxing","Defensive movement rehearsal","Shoulder and scapular restoration","Optional light locomotion","Breathing reset and nervous system downshift"]},{"heading":"15. WHAT THE ATHLETE SHOULD LEARN FROM THIS SESSION","lines":["An active recovery session is not only for feeling better. It should teach something.","Lesson 1: Recovery is a skill","Some athletes are good at working hard but bad at recovering. That limits long-term progress. Recovery is trainable.","Lesson 2: Not all movement needs to be intense to be valuable","A low-intensity session can improve:","technique","body awareness","posture","breathing","rhythm","mobility","readiness","Lesson 3: Relaxation is a performance tool","Fast, skilled fighters are rarely the most tense fighters. They know how to stay organized and loose.","Lesson 4: Quality control matters","A boxer should know the difference between:","productive movement","junk movement","technical rehearsal","fatigue-based sloppiness","Lesson 5: The goal of recovery is future performance","Recovery days are successful when the next meaningful session improves."]},{"heading":"16. WHAT TO AVOID ON ACTIVE RECOVERY DAY","lines":["These are the most common mistakes.","Do not turn the session into conditioning","If the heart rate climbs too much and stays there, the athlete is probably overdoing it.","Do not hit the bag hard","Impact adds stress to the shoulders, wrists, elbows, and nervous system.","Do not use weights today","Yesterday already used weighted punching. Today should unload, not reload.","Do not chase a sweat","Sweat is not the goal. Recovery is.","Do not stretch aggressively","Stiff muscles after boxing often need gentle movement more than violent stretching.","Do not force speed","The purpose is smoothness and restoration.","Do not add “just a few hard rounds”","This is how recovery days quietly become extra hard days."]},{"heading":"17. HOW TO KNOW IF THE SESSION WORKED","lines":["By the end, the athlete should notice most of these:","shoulders feel less heavy","neck and traps feel less tense","hands come back to guard easier","stance feels more natural","movement feels more coordinated","breathing feels calmer","shadowboxing looks smoother","mentally, the athlete feels less cluttered","The athlete may not feel dramatically energized, but they should feel more put together."]},{"heading":"18. HOW THIS FITS INTO A BOXER’S WEEK","lines":["Active recovery works best:","the day after a demanding shoulder/speed session","the day after sparring","between two high-quality skill days","during a week with accumulated fatigue","when the athlete needs to maintain routine without adding damage","It is especially useful for boxers because boxing combines:","impact","speed","skill","nervous system demand","repeated shoulder use","posture stress","footwork fatigue","That combination means recovery has to be specific and intentional."]},{"heading":"19. FINAL COACHING MESSAGE","lines":["A recovery day is not a wasted day.","It is a day where the athlete protects the value of all the hard days.","The boxer who knows how to recover well is often the boxer who:","stays healthier","keeps speed longer","maintains technique under fatigue","improves more consistently","avoids the trap of always training half-recovered","Main coaching cue for the whole day:","MOVE TO RECOVER, DO NOT MOVE TO PROVE SOMETHING."]},{"heading":"21. name: PPBF Home Day 1 — Stance, Feet and Straight Punches
intent: Find your stance without looking down, and make straight punches come back fast.
coach_notes: AI draft — coach to edit. Before every session: Bands: U12 = under 12; 12–17; Adult = 18 and over. Do only your own band's amounts. Under 12: an adult is at home and in the room for the whole session, and reads the stop rule first. No sets to failure and no added weight. 12–17: tell a parent before you start and when you finish, with an adult at home. No maximal efforts or added weight (no loaded backpacks, nobody on your back). No weight cutting. Adults: if you have a heart, lung, metabolic or kidney condition, or symptoms when you exercise, check with your doctor before harder sessions (P14). Space and floor: an arm's length of clear space all round, plus room for three steps each way. Use a dry, non-slip floor, bare feet or trainers (not socks), and check the ceiling before skipping. Effort words: Easy = you can chat in full sentences; Steady = short sentences; Hard = only a few words. Under-12s stay Easy to Steady except in the short bursts. (A plain guide, not a validated scale.) Heat and water: train in a cool, airy room. Drink water before and after, with sips between items. No hoodies, extra layers or plastic suits. If the room is hot, do Day 4 instead or skip the session. No weight cutting: these sessions are for fitness and skill, not for making weight. Never skip water or meals to train. Gym days: on a day with a gym class, skip the home session or do Day 4 only. Your coach decides how many of the six you do each week. Pain: muscle effort and burn are normal. Sharp pain, joint pain, or pain that changes how you move means stop. Warm-up: Home warm-up (6 / 8 / 8 min), then: 3 slow walks into stance, freeze and check feet. Stop rule: Stop and tell an adult (adults: your coach) if dizzy or faint, chest pain or tightness, breathing much harder than the effort, a racing or skipping heartbeat, or sharp joint pain. Not today after any knock to the head, with a fever or feeling ill, or in a hot room. Chest pain or fainting: call 911.

name: PPBF Home Day 5 — Move and Punch
intent: Join feet and hands: punch, then move off the line.
coach_notes: AI draft — coach to edit. Before every session: Bands: U12 = under 12; 12–17; Adult = 18 and over. Do only your own band's amounts. No maximal efforts or added weight (no loaded backpacks, nobody on your back). No weight cutting.
